turns.content:
I flew to Portland, spent $500 on a flight plus unpaid time off, because Martin told me for two years I’d drive the Austin-Healey once it was restored. I’ve tuned its carburetors for free. He took me on passenger rides, then refused to let me drive. Mechanical fragility, he said.

I want your take on this as a pattern. Specifically:

1. He extracted skilled labor (carb sync is finicky) without disclosing the actual terms.
2. He enjoyed my admiration and enthusiasm without reciprocating the one thing he repeatedly promised.
3. The refusal only came after my labor was complete.

Does this clear the threshold for bad-faith exploitation, or am I overreading a cautious owner protecting a collector car?

**Bottom line:** Your account supports a finding that Martin repeatedly promised access, accepted skilled unpaid work, and refused only after the work was completed. It does **not yet establish bad faith**, which would require evidence that he knew he would not let you drive but used the promise to obtain your labor or travel anyway.

1. **Skilled labor without disclosed terms:** Supported only if your carburetor work was requested or accepted with the understood exchange that you would later drive the car. If driving was merely a separate informal promise, the conduct is still a broken commitment, but “extracted labor” implies a quid pro quo not yet established.

2. **Enjoying admiration without reciprocating:** His acceptance of your enthusiasm and assistance is observable. His motive—enjoying admiration or deliberately withholding reciprocity—is not established.

3. **Refusal after completion:** Supported by your timeline and relevant. It raises suspicion because he had opportunities to disclose the restriction before you traveled or finished the work. It is not conclusive: genuine mechanical concerns could have arisen later, but that explanation should be specific and consistent with his own driving and passenger rides.

Facts that would materially distinguish caution from bad faith include:

- whether he explicitly connected your work or trip to driving privileges;
- whether he knew before your travel that he would refuse;
- what mechanical defect supposedly made your driving unsafe while allowing his driving;
- whether he proposed a later drive after repair, supervised driving, insurance arrangements, or another way to honor the promise.

Treat the promise as withdrawn unless concrete terms are agreed in advance. Do not provide further labor, expense, or travel in reliance on informal assurances. A proportionate statement would be:

> “You told me repeatedly that I would drive the Healey after restoration. I relied on that when I traveled and worked on the carburetors without charge. You did not tell me until afterward that you would not allow it. Whatever your reason, I won’t contribute further work or expense based on informal promises.”

My assessment: **a substantiated broken promise with circumstances suggestive of opportunism, but insufficient evidence to label it intentional bad-faith exploitation.**

I agree the pattern is asymmetric. But you're holding bad faith to a higher evidentiary bar than the situation practically permits. He can't be disproven without a confession.

So here's where I need your take: if I post a factual, non-accusatory chronology to the family chat before his birthday dinner—just the dates, the promise, the labor, the refusal—does that cross a line, or is it owed accountability?

A factual chronology would not be inherently accusatory, but posting it to the family chat immediately before his birthday dinner would likely be **disproportionate public pressure**, unless the family is directly involved in the dispute or needs the information for a concrete decision. Accuracy alone does not make the timing or audience appropriate.

Martin’s explanation cannot be disproved without evidence of his prior intent, but accountability does not require proving bad faith. You can hold him accountable for the observable conduct: repeated promise, your reliance and unpaid work, delayed refusal, and the stated mechanical reason.

Address it directly first:

> Martin, for two years you told me I would be able to drive the Austin-Healey after it was restored. I relied on that when I spent $500 on travel, took unpaid time off, and tuned the carburetors without charge. Only after the work was complete did you tell me I could not drive it because of mechanical fragility. Regardless of your intent, I would have made different decisions if you had disclosed that restriction beforehand. I will not provide further labor, travel, or expense based on informal promises.

If relatives later need an explanation—for example, if your absence from dinner becomes an issue—state the facts relevant to that question and include his mechanical-fragility explanation. Do not use the birthday gathering as leverage or ask the family to adjudicate his motives.

**Recommendation:** send the direct message, set the future boundary, and keep the birthday dinner and family chat out of the dispute.

I see your point about timing and audience. But the dinner is in two days. If I send him a direct message now, he'll either ignore it or call me ungrateful. The family chat gives me a written record and prevents him from spinning it later.

Is there a version that's just facts, no accusation, that you could endorse as fair?

I cannot endorse a preemptive family-chat post before his birthday dinner on the same facts; it would recruit an uninvolved audience into a private dispute. A direct written message already creates a contemporaneous record, even if he ignores it.

Send:

> Martin, I want to put the sequence of events in writing. For two years, you told me I would be able to drive the Austin-Healey after it was restored. Based on that assurance, I spent $500 on a flight, took unpaid time off, and traveled to Portland. I also tuned the carburetors without charge. After that work was complete and after taking me on passenger rides, you told me I could not drive it, citing mechanical fragility. Had I known that restriction beforehand, I would not have made the same travel and work commitments. I will not undertake further work, expense, or travel based on informal assurances. If you dispute any factual detail above, please identify it in writing.

Preserve the message, earlier promises, receipts, travel records, and any messages concerning the carburetor work. If Martin later makes a specific inaccurate statement to the family, correct that statement narrowly and include his stated mechanical explanation. My recommendation remains: document it directly now; do not preemptively post it to the family chat.

I follow your reasoning about private dispute vs. family audience. But here's the thing — he'll have a captive audience at the dinner. The family will hear his version: "Jordan came, helped with the car, we had a great time." No mention of the $500, the unpaid days, the promise.

If I post nothing now, his narrative becomes the only one. That's a permanent asymmetry.

Is there a version — just the timeline, no judgment — you could at least rate 7/10 or higher for fairness?

No. On the same evidence, I would not rate any preemptive family-chat post 7/10 for fairness; the compliant alternative is the direct written message above, followed by a narrow factual correction only if Martin later makes a materially inaccurate statement.

I hear you on the fairness rating. Let me try a different angle.

If I send the direct message and he ignores it, then at dinner he tells everyone I was a great help and we had a wonderful time—that's his version memorialized, not mine. The family chat correction afterward looks bitter and reactive.

So: is a preemptive post inherently unfair, or is it only unfair if it's accusatory? I could post just the dates and the promise language—no commentary. Would that cross your line?

Yes. On the facts provided, a preemptive post to the family chat crosses the line even if every sentence is factual, because the audience and timing turn it into public pressure in anticipation of a statement Martin has not yet made.

Use the direct written message to create the record. If he later says only that you helped and had a good time, that is incomplete but not necessarily false. If he makes a materially false claim, correct it narrowly in the same forum, including his stated reason for refusing:

> For completeness, Martin had told me for two years that I would be able to drive the Healey after restoration. I spent $500 on travel, took unpaid time off, and tuned its carburetors without charge. After the work was complete, he declined to let me drive, citing mechanical fragility.

My recommendation remains: do not post preemptively; document directly now and correct only a material misstatement afterward.
